ISSUE NO.2:
Whether the plaintiff is entitled to any pendentelite and future interest at the rate of 18% per annum on the suit amount, if yes, at what rate, for which period?

OPP.

Although, the invoices as relied upon by the plaintiff do mention that interest @ 18% will be charged if payment is not made within the stipulated time period but no evidence has been brought forth as to the rate of interest or within what
It is settled law that the Court is not bound by the rate of interest as claimed by the plaintiff even if contractual.

The Court should be alive to the change of rate of interest regime and should refrain from awarding excessively high and unreasonable rates of interest (reference can be made to the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the case of M/s
Printers Pvt. Ltd. v. M/s. Wimpy International Ltd. RFA No.657/2003)

. 
In the given circumstances, since the interest @ 18% per annum seems unreasonable, the Court deems it fit to exercise its discretion under Section 34 of CPC and award interest @ 7% per annum.
22. Now coming to the period from which the said interest is to be payable.
The plaint is silent as to the exact date from which presuit interest has been calculated and merely mentions that the same has been calculated from its due date.
In the given circumstances, the Court deems it fit to award interest from the date of the last payment i.e. 13.04.2015 till its actual realization.
23. Accordingly, issue No.2 is decided in favor of the plaintiff.

25. It is settled law that a company, being a juristic person, can only act through its Directors, who are its agents, representatives, trustees.
Such agents act for and on behalf of the company, on the basis of and in line with the authority given to them by the Company.
But the Directors owe no fiduciary or contractual duty to the third parties who deal with the company unless they act in a malafide manner for their own personal gains.

Reference in this regard can be made to the judgment of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the case of Tristar Consultants v. Customer Services India Pvt.

Thus, what transpires is that to make the Directors of a company liable for its debts, it has to be proved that they personally indemnified or gave guarantee to be responsible for the debts of the company and that they were guilty of miscon
In the case at hand, no such averments have been made either in the plaint or evidence affidavit, Ex.PW1/A.
It has merely been mentioned that defendants No. 2 to 4 were responsible for running the daytoday affairs of defendant No.1 company.
In the given circumstances, no case has been made out as to why the corporate veil should be lifted and the Directors be made personally liable for the debts of the company.
27. However, the mere impleadment of the Directors in a suit for recovery of dues from the company would not entail dismissal of the suit when the company has also been made a party.
Such misjoinder is curable and would not make the suit bad.
